scenes.tts: Insulin never crosses the cell membrane. Yet within minutes, a muscle cell pulls glucose out of the blood and stores it as glycogen. The signal runs from the receptor to one kinase, called Akt. Before insulin arrives, Akt drifts in the cytosol, inactive. How does a message from outside reach it?
scenes.visual: Insulin lands on the membrane and is stopped by a red bar; glucose crosses and becomes glycogen. Akt drifts in the cytosol, inactive. A dashed path of question-mark boxes joins insulin to Akt.
scenes.narration: Insulin never crosses the cell membrane. Yet within minutes, a muscle cell pulls glucose out of the blood and stores it as glycogen. The signal runs from the receptor to one kinase, called Akt. Before insulin arrives, Akt drifts in the cytosol, inactive. How does a message from outside reach it?

scenes.tts: Insulin binds its receptor, which is a tyrosine kinase. The receptor adds phosphates to its own tyrosines, and then to those of a docking protein, I R S one. I R S one is held at the membrane beside the receptor, and has a long tail with many tyrosines. Once the receptor has phosphorylated that tail, proteins with S H 2 domains dock on it. An S H 2 domain binds a phosphorylated tyrosine, and one such protein is P I 3 kinase.
scenes.caption: Insulin binds its receptor, which is a tyrosine kinase. The receptor adds phosphates to its own tyrosines, and then to those of a docking protein, IRS-1. IRS-1 is held at the membrane beside the receptor, and has a long tail with many tyrosines. Once the receptor has phosphorylated that tail, proteins with SH2 domains dock on it. An SH2 domain binds a phosphorylated tyrosine, and one such protein is PI 3-kinase.
scenes.visual: The question-mark path is replaced by the real relay: insulin sits on a receptor, phosphates pass to IRS-1 and down its tail, pink SH2 cups close on them, and one docked protein becomes PI 3-kinase.
scenes.narration: Insulin binds its receptor, which is a tyrosine kinase. The receptor adds phosphates to its own tyrosines, and then to those of a docking protein, IRS-1. IRS-1 is held at the membrane beside the receptor, and has a long tail with many tyrosines. Once the receptor has phosphorylated that tail, proteins with SH2 domains dock on it. An SH2 domain binds a phosphorylated tyrosine, and one such protein is PI 3-kinase.

scenes.tts: P I 3 kinase now sits at the membrane, where its substrate is. That substrate is a lipid called P I P 2. The catalytic subunit of P I 3 kinase adds a phosphate to the 3 position of the lipid. The product is P I P 3. P I P 3 is a membrane address.
scenes.caption: PI 3-kinase now sits at the membrane, where its substrate is. That substrate is a lipid called PIP2. The catalytic subunit of PI 3-kinase adds a phosphate to the 3 position of the lipid. The product is PIP3. PIP3 is a membrane address.
scenes.visual: Zoomed in on the inner face of the membrane: a row of PIP2 lipid heads, PI 3-kinase beside them. A phosphate lands on one head, then on the rest; the row is labelled PIP3, a membrane address.
scenes.narration: PI 3-kinase now sits at the membrane, where its substrate is. That substrate is a lipid called PIP2. The catalytic subunit of PI 3-kinase adds a phosphate to the 3 position of the lipid. The product is PIP3. PIP3 is a membrane address.

scenes.tts: Akt has a P H domain at its amino end. This domain binds P I P 3. So Akt leaves the cytosol. The lipid holds it against the membrane. Akt is now at the address.
scenes.caption: Akt has a PH domain at its amino end. This domain binds PIP3. So Akt leaves the cytosol. The lipid holds it against the membrane. Akt is now at the address.
scenes.visual: A pink cup grows on Akt's left end and is named. Akt rises from the cytosol and the cup closes on a PIP3 phosphate, holding Akt against the membrane.
scenes.narration: Akt has a PH domain at its amino end. This domain binds PIP3. So Akt leaves the cytosol. The lipid holds it against the membrane. Akt is now at the address.

scenes.tts: A second kinase, P D K one, has its own P H domain, so the lipid holds it there too. P D K one adds a phosphate to a threonine in the activation loop of Akt. That is the loop a kinase must set before it works. A separate kinase complex, m T O R C two, adds a second phosphate near the tail, on a serine. The first phosphate does most of the work, the second adds to it, and together they give full activity.
scenes.caption: A second kinase, PDK1, has its own PH domain, so the lipid holds it there too. PDK1 adds a phosphate to a threonine in the activation loop of Akt. That is the loop a kinase must set before it works. A separate kinase complex, mTORC2, adds a second phosphate near the tail, on a serine. The first phosphate does most of the work, the second adds to it, and together they give full activity.
scenes.visual: PDK1 arrives and its own pink cup closes on a neighbouring PIP3. It passes a phosphate to the loop on Akt; mTORC2 passes a second to Akt's tail. The first badge is drawn larger; Akt turns green.
scenes.narration: A second kinase, PDK1, has its own PH domain, so the lipid holds it there too. PDK1 adds a phosphate to a threonine in the activation loop of Akt. That is the loop a kinase must set before it works. A separate kinase complex, mTORC2, adds a second phosphate near the tail, on a serine. scenes.tts: Why does Akt need a lipid and two phosphates? Each is a check: Akt is on only where P I P 3 has been made. With no insulin, normal Akt stays in the cytosol. But give Akt a permanent fatty acid anchor, and it sits at the membrane, gains both phosphates, and is active. Keep this rule: the main job of P I P 3 is to put Akt in the right place.

scenes.visual: Three ticks mark the lipid grip and the two phosphates. Two panels, both with no insulin: normal Akt stays inactive in the cytosol; Akt with a fatty acid anchor hangs from the membrane, gains both phosphates and turns green. The anchor is replaced by a PIP3 grip.
